inline.s: Sit quietly, let yourself think carefully, and reflect on the Buddha’s spirit of compassion; then your own inner wisdom will give you the right answer.
Beliefs Learned in Childhood

Some beliefs learned in childhood are positive and beneficial, of help to us throughout our whole lives. For example: "Before crossing the street, look both ways, and do not cross while cars are coming."
and so on.
There are also other beliefs that are useful only when we are small; once we grow up they no longer suit us. For example: "Do not believe what other people say."
and so on. Reaching out to others is something we should no longer fear after adulthood; if we never trust others, a person becomes lonely and isolated, and his development in society is limited.

Boys should not cry" and "Girls should not run and jump" are also beliefs that adults instill in children. Such beliefs often produce men who hide their feelings and women who love to sit still and never move about.

If adults teach a child, "This world is a very cold and heartless place," then the child will take it as truth and believe that everyone in the world is heartless; so he will not dare to associate with others, and will often remain so even when grown.

On the other hand, if adults teach a child, "As long as you are good to others, they will be good to you," then the child’s behavior will be different — as an adult more ready to accept others and to give of his love.

Some adults routinely scold their children: "It’s all your fault!" Scolding of this kind keeps a child perpetually uneasy; whatever happens, he thinks it must be his fault again, so that on reaching adulthood he remains the same, becoming a person who cringes and dares not act.

If a person believed in childhood that he was unimportant, then in every circumstance he will be the one who keeps to the sidelines, even when grown. If his family always ignored him, then when he is an adult he will likewise feel that, amid the crowd, he seems not to exist.

Children in the first grade often have difficulty learning and make their teachers work hard to teach them. So some children, after being blamed by the teacher, come to believe they must be stupid, and plant the banner of stupidity forever in their own hearts.

Some people have very poor childhood environments, which lead them to believe that no one loves them and leave them very lonely as adults. Even if they bring a friend or a love into their lives, these do not last.

Some families give children the belief that "people are never satisfied." Such a belief makes him feel, once grown, that the clothes in his closet are always too few and the money he earns never enough; and he lives perpetually in a state of discontented resentment.
One patient said his family had always believed that nothing turned out well, and felt that things would only grow worse and never better; and so he was himself filled with negative beliefs.

He even hurt his knee while playing ball, and it felt like a great calamity. He went everywhere to see doctors, consulting many different physicians; his knee, he felt, kept getting worse. After a great while, when his knee had fully recovered, he never played ball again. Playing ball had been his favorite sport and pastime, yet he had to give it up — he feared that playing again would bring about something worse.

Another person was influenced from childhood by his father, who taught him, while he was still small, to grab everything ahead of others, or else he would lose the chance and even end up with nothing. So when he grew up he would not help others; even queuing to buy theater tickets, he insisted on pushing ahead of everyone, ignoring all order. Because of this, many people did not want to be his friend, and he suffered great mental distress.

The only way to deal with the negative beliefs learned in childhood is to discard them completely: learn from the Buddha and build a new, positive outlook on life. If you believe in the Buddha, all your problems will be resolved.
We often say: "I am who I am; I have always been this way." We also say: "Things are just like this; they cannot change."
These two statements sound very true, but in fact they are only beliefs, not facts. Yet if we believe them forever, they harden into stubborn facts.

What we ordinarily believe is usually only the opinions of others; but we gather many of those opinions into our own belief system. There these beliefs mingle with our other beliefs and become our own.
Many people, waking in the morning and finding it raining outside, immediately think: "Oh, what terrible weather today!"

In fact, a rainy day is not bad at all; it is simply that the air is damp. If we have proper rain gear, wear suitable shoes, and change our attitude toward rainy days, then a rainy day can become a very pleasant day — at least never worse than any other. Even if you find no poetry in it, you can see that it fills the reservoirs and benefits the grass, trees, and crops; and on rainy days there is less dust in the streets.

But if we persist in believing that a rainy day is a bad day, then every time it rains our hearts sink and we become quite gloomy. We resist the rainy day instead of learning to go along with this present moment.
In truth, the weather is neither "good" nor "bad"; weather is simply weather. But if we regard a rainy day as "bad" and let it affect our mood, then a rainy day truly becomes "bad."

To attain a joyful life, one must first have joyful thoughts; to have a vigorous life, one must first have vigorous thoughts; to have a life brimming with loving-kindness, one must first have thoughts brimming with loving-kindness.
A person’s thoughts lead his actions; sow what "cause," and when the "conditions" ripen, you reap what "fruit."
A New Beginning at Every Moment

I want to tell you again and again: the focus of power is always upon this present moment. Every minute and every second before us can never remain standing still. And so, in this present moment, we can change our minds at once.
Even if we are ill, trapped in negative thoughts, forever hating ourselves, and long beset by financial hardship, it matters not; in this present moment we can begin to change everything at once.
All problems can be wiped away at their root, so that they are no longer a reality of the future; as long as you are willing, you can surely accomplish it.
Remember: in our minds, it is ourselves who do the thinking; in our world, it is ourselves who are the true power!
Our past thoughts and beliefs created all our past experiences.
Our present thoughts and beliefs will create all our encounters in the next moment, the next month, and the next year.
It is not "fate" that guides you; it is "thoughts and beliefs" that guide you.
A monk who had not a penny to his name was able to build a grand temple because he first had the thought and conviction, and then acted upon them, so that finally it became reality.

Dear readers, here I offer you the most precious counsel I have, an honest advice drawn from many years of living. If you do not wish to listen, you may refuse to change and continue to choose your old ways of thinking, keeping all your problems entirely intact.
I say this in all sincerity: in our world, we ourselves are the only power! Whatever thoughts and actions we choose will one by one become the reality of the future!
If only you begin a new course of action in this present moment, then every instant is a fresh beginning — and this is entirely possible! For friends with problems, this is truly good news!
Friend! Make up your mind and begin your change from this present moment — begin a new life!
Is It Really So?

If you are musing over something, first grasp hold of the thought you have right now. What exactly are you thinking at this very moment? Because your thoughts can truly produce actions in you, consider carefully: do you really want the thought you just had to become a fact?
If your thought is one of anxiety, anger, grief, revenge, or fear, you must be all the more watchful — think it clearly through! Think of what outcomes that unwholesome thought may bring!

Though grasping our thoughts is not so easy — they shift so swiftly, like flashes of lightning — from this moment on we must know what we are thinking. If you find that your thoughts are only negative intentions, cut them off at once and do not let them carry on.
You can change at once, choosing positive thoughts and commanding the negative intentions to depart with firm resolve.

Every guest in a buffet restaurant can face all the food on offer and choose from it what he likes. In the same way, every person who works with his thoughts can choose his own thoughts. And choosing thoughts matters more than choosing food: food is only good-tasting or not, whereas thoughts can shape a person’s whole future course of life.

Therefore, if you choose thoughts that will create problems and suffering for you, that is extremely unwise — even worse than choosing food that upsets your stomach. Of course, unavoidably, we all occasionally make wrong choices; but to err once is enough. Once we know that certain foods disagree with our body, we do not choose them again. In the same way, choosing thoughts must not be an endless string of mistakes; thoughts that create problems and suffering are already too much to entertain even once.

In my early years I met a minister named Charles Polk, who often repeated to us students: "When a problem arises, we should not act upon it at once; instead we should first come to know that problem well."
Our mind can create our future. Therefore, whenever we are dissatisfied with a situation, we must use our mind to change it. Moreover, we must begin changing our mind in this present moment.

For example, you have a good friend. He has always been kind to you, but suddenly the two of you disagree over some matter and there is even a conflict. As a result he wins and you lose, so you seethe with indignation, your mind full of resentful thoughts toward him; you even think of taking revenge on him to vent your anger. Though you also realize that attacking him would only hurt you both and ruin your friendship for good, bringing you no benefit whatsoever, you are still bent on letting off this anger and will not rest until you have had your way

Your mind by now is like a wild horse, charging about in all directions. If you do not immediately rein it in at the cliff’s edge and change at once, then all the friendship between you and your old friend will be destroyed by your actions.

Understand the problem" means to think it clearly through: who is truly right and who is truly wrong? Why did he win and you lose? Now that you have lost, must you take revenge on the winner? Is the thought of preferring mutual ruin a matter of rash impulse, or is it right? Even if your old friend truly erred this time, could you not forgive him for now and wait for him to come to his own realization? Must you behave like a petty person? Why not act like a noble one?
When you at last can change your own mind, the tragedy of a broken friendship will not come about.

In truth, many of the things you believe are against you are not really so. You must use your thought, wisdom, and compassion to understand why others act as they do, and so turn enemies into friends and renew good connections.
If you treat a friend as an enemy, the friend will truly become an enemy.
If you treat an enemy as a friend, the enemy will also truly become a friend.
All dharmas are mind-only" — the Buddha’s teaching is quite correct; your mind determines everything about you.
Deciding to Change
Now, many people raise their hands and surrender in fear to their own worries and problems; most people cling to everything and refuse to attempt change.
Many people will say: "I do not think I can change, and I see no hope of changing, so I do not want to try."

Many others will say: "I think it is better not to change, for I am already used to living in suffering and know how to accept it, even though I do not like suffering. Yet that is still better than going against it, because if I resist it, it may grow worse and become more than I can bear."
In fact, resentment is of no use at all. When something bad happens, we resent it; once the resentment has passed, still other bad things occur, and so we resent again
and in this endless cycle we can never rise above our suffering.
What use is resentment? It is a foolish reaction, a response to life that refuses to understand.
We must earnestly ask ourselves: why is it that so many bad things happen, so that people cannot help feeling resentment?

I believe there must be some belief in your heart that is not right, and that is what gives rise to so much worry and dejection, drawing others to trouble you from time to time. Why do you not change your thoughts and conduct, so as to stop bad things from happening and never need to resent again?

Even if bad things have already happened, you should reflect on the single word the Buddha taught you — forbearance — and meet people with compassion, dealing with problems with compassion. That is the true way to be released from suffering.
As you treat others, so others treat you; if you are generous toward others’ faults, others will also be generous toward you when you go wrong.
If you truly wish to know how stubborn you are, you need only consider whether you are a person who is willing to change, and you will know clearly.

Every one of us hopes to change our life for the better, to handle everything more aptly, more properly, and more easily. Yet, however much we wish it, we often cannot truly change. We would rather have others change to suit us than change ourselves to suit everything.

If you cannot change for your own sake, how can others be expected to change themselves for you? Changing oneself is not easy, yet it is by no means beyond our reach. We need only begin from within ourselves: first change our old ways of thinking, then change the tone with which we speak to others; and spontaneously, the circumstances around us will change as well.

Change your thinking and change how you speak, and you can change your life and make everything better. It sounds easy, yet in practice it is often far from easy, because everyone has his measure of stubbornness — more or less — and also the matter of perseverance — whether he can hold on.

Take me for example: I have always been rather stubborn. Even now, whenever my life calls for a fresh decision and a change, that bit of stubbornness rises from deep within me to the surface, making me resist change and hold on to my old thoughts, so that for a while I become once more an opinionated, resentful, isolated person.
Even someone like me, who has worked at self-improvement for years, is like this — which shows how very hard it is to deal with human stubbornness.

I have made dealing with stubbornness one of my own courses of study and practice it constantly. Whenever stubbornness arises, I never fail to tell myself: I am at an important turning point in my life; I must not indulge in slackness and let stubbornness triumph. Since I have decided to make changes in my life, I must bring about new thoughts and new actions! At that moment I turn deep into my own within, peeling away the layers of old thought one by one, so that each layer of old thought gives way to new thought.

In this process I often meet with difficulty, because some old thoughts are easily peeled away, while others are as stubborn as trying to move a great stone with a feather — the old thought refuses to stir in the least and stands unshaken.

People are often barred from the road to success by serious problems; if they do not overcome them, they will know only failure forever. In replacing the old with the new, the more stubborn an old thought, the more it becomes a stumbling block in life, so it must be removed. Recognize it clearly, confront it earnestly, and with perseverance you will win the victory.

There is one thing we must understand clearly: recognizing that our past thoughts and beliefs were mistaken does not mean that we were not good people in the past. There is no need to grieve and rage over our past; on the contrary, in this present moment of improvement, we should gladly celebrate.
Let us say it earnestly: "I am willing to change."
Say it again and again: "I am willing to change, I am willing to change." When we say this, it is best to place our hand over our chest to show our resolve.

Our chest is a very important center of power in our body; this center can help us put change into practice. By saying and doing this, you acknowledge that you are in the very process of seeking change.
We should know that in our lives there are indeed certain situations that need to be changed. At such a time we should let them change, and not suppress them.

Pay attention to the places where we are unwilling to change, for those are very likely exactly what we most need to change. When you set about it, you will find that the "conditions" that help us succeed are slowly gathering together.
When we say, sincerely and repeatedly, "I am willing to change," our situation truly begins to change.
The Path of Carrying Out Change
We should not only lift ourselves a step higher in thought and intention, but also renew ourselves one by one in other respects.
We should attend to improvement in the spiritual, improvement in the psychological, and above all improvement in the physical.
A true process of healing should give heed to body, mind, and spirit all at once. However, one may begin from any of the three.

Some begin with the psychological, taking courses in psychology or psychotherapy; some begin with the spiritual, learning to sit in meditation and regularly recite the sutras; some begin with the physical, taking up exercise and watching their nutrition.
This is like cleaning our house: it does not matter which room we tackle first, so long as the whole house is cleaned.
If we can advance on all three at once, so much the better. Doing so can shorten the period of physical decline and restore health all the sooner.

An old Chinese proverb says that "illness enters through the mouth," holding that many diseases arise from improper diet; hence there are many prohibitions regarding food. In daily life people value "food tonics," and after illness they not only take medicine but also observe "dietary restraints." These sayings and practices may seem quite "old-fashioned," yet analyzed with a modern mind they are very "scientific" and entirely in accord with the way of health. Indeed, many of people’s illnesses are often caused by improper diet. Common sense tells us that inadequate nutrition certainly undermines health, while excessive nutrition also brings on many diseases. Moreover there is the matter of "food allergy," which has already aroused widespread concern.

In the past, people knew only that seafood such as fish, shrimp, and crab caused food allergies, and that other foods did not. But with the advance of medicine it has been confirmed that the foods capable of causing allergies number well over a hundred kinds. "Food allergy" is not merely a matter of an itching skin; it can be severe enough to cost a person his life. For this reason I do not lightly draw up lists of food nutrition for anyone, unless I know precisely how his "food allergies" stand. Some foods suit certain people but not others; other foods suit still others but not some; each case must be studied in detail, and we cannot treat all alike.

There was a patient who had always been fond of drinking milk. When he later developed a stomach ulcer, he was all the more convinced that he should eat more fluids to improve his condition; so whenever he felt thirsty or slightly hungry, he would use milk to quench his thirst and satisfy his hunger. As a result, though he took the doctor’s medicine, the diarrhea did not improve but gradually grew worse — more violent and more frequent — and he grew thinner day by day. The doctor told him that he must not drink too much milk, but he would not listen, believing that without milk his body would be all the more lacking in nourishment. He stopped the medicine, which had done nothing for his diarrhea, and came to my clinic to see me. I asked him to stop drinking milk entirely from that very day; in only a day or two his severe diarrhea cleared up at once and his body grew sturdy and strong again. For this patient the saying that "illness enters through the mouth" was altogether apt. Examples of the same kind are too many to count.

If a person indiscriminately gives himself "nutrition," bad consequences often follow; so one cannot be too careful. Yet ordinary food is not so frightening as to make everyone ill. The main matter is whether the person who eats it does so appropriately. If the amount eaten is not excessive, there is certainly no great danger; on this point you may set your mind at rest.

My own view on nutrition is very simple: as long as each day you eat many foods of different colors, that is enough. If a certain food always leaves you feeling unwell after eating it, you need to give it special attention; once it has been confirmed and proved again and again to be bad for you, make up your mind never to eat it again.

If you are a parent with young children, you must all the more take your children’s diet into account and observe it carefully. In general, meat carries the most toxins; even if you are not allergic to it, you should not eat too great a quantity. It is best to replace it with protein-rich legumes from the plant kingdom. This also explains why so many more people are becoming vegetarian now — that is the very reason. The pity is that many are accustomed to eating meat, and to give it up all at once is not easy for them; in such a case we let things take their natural course and go slowly. I believe that once people’s ideas change, they will gradually put it into practice.

There are also many Westerners who, after eating a vegetarian diet for a while, find themselves becoming anemic and so have to return to eating meat. This is because in their markets the variety of vegetarian foods is too limited, so they cannot take in complete nutrition. I believe such situations will change with need in the future: as long as food merchants put their minds to it, things will be different.
No matter in what area a person changes, there will be a day or two when the body feels unwell — whether it is a change of diet, a change of one’s system of thought, or beginning to sit in meditation

it is all the same. It may even seem much worse than before the change. This is a necessary phenomenon of the old giving way to the new, like preparing to scrub a cooking pot that has long been scorched and is hard to clean. We put hot water and detergent into the pot and let it soak, and only then begin to scour it; and at that moment the pot truly becomes a mess, looking even worse than before we set about cleaning it.
But if you keep on scouring, before very long you will have a pot that seems brand new.
It is the same with tidying up one’s mental system.

When we steep ourselves in new intentions and thoughts, all our former turbid thoughts rise to the surface for you to witness. But as long as you keep building new, wholesome thoughts, before very long you will have an entirely new system of thought, no longer disordered and unwholesome as before — truly making everything about you fresh and new.

For our own good we all wish to change what is bad in our lives; whatever the method, so long as it helps us, we should accept it. Here is one method — many people have used it, and I have used it myself. The method is this: tell yourself that you are willing to change.
Stand before the mirror and tell yourself: "I am willing to change."
Doing this gives rise to great power, because you have declared your resolve. But if you feel hesitant, or are simply unwilling to change, then ask yourself why it should be so.
What old belief is it that you are still clinging to?
